claims.text: AWS offers Elastic Cloud Compute (EC2) as its compute service.
Azure provides Virtual Machines as its compute service.
GCP offers Compute Engine as its compute service.
AWS EC2 offers various instance types, including general purpose, compute optimized, memory optimized, accelerated compute, and storage optimized.
GCP Compute Engine supports general purpose VMs, compute optimized, memory optimized, and accelerated VMs, as well as burstable or shared core VMs.
Azure Virtual Machines offers general purpose VMs, compute and memory optimized VMs, accelerator optimized VMs (GPU type), storage optimized VMs, and burstable options.
All three cloud providers (AWS, Azure, GCP) offer auto-scaling capabilities for their compute services.
AWS provides Amazon Simple Storage Service (S3) as its object storage service.
Azure provides Azure Blob Storage as its object storage service.
GCP provides Cloud Storage as its object storage service.
AWS provides Amazon Elastic Block Store (EBS) as its block storage service.
Azure provides Managed Disks as its block storage service.
GCP provides Persistent Disk as its block storage service.
AWS provides Amazon Elastic File System (EFS) and FSx as its file storage services.
Azure provides Azure Files as its file storage service.
GCP provides Filestore as its file storage service.
All three cloud providers (AWS, Azure, GCP) offer storage services with features like versioning, encryption at rest, and fine-grained security.
AWS, Azure, and GCP offer archive storage tiers with different pricing, such as S3 Glacier, Azure Archive Storage, and Cloud Storage Archive.
AWS, Azure, and GCP differ in their virtual network isolation implementations, with AWS using VPCs, Azure using Virtual Networks, and GCP using a global VPC model.
GCP's VPC is global and spans across regions, whereas AWS and Azure have regional VPCs/VNets that require explicit peering or transit networking for inter-region connectivity.
AWS uses Transit Gateway to simplify multi-VPC communication, Azure uses Virtual WAN for large-scale network management, and GCP uses Shared VPC for efficient resource sharing across projects.

The three cloud providers have different default network structures: AWS uses VPCs, subnets, and route tables; Azure starts with subnets, NSGs, and route decisions; GCP's global network abstraction simplifies subnet design but requires careful planning for routing and shared services.

GCP's global load balancer uses a single anycast IP address to route users to the nearest healthy backend across regions, differing from AWS and Azure's regional load balancers with separate global routing layers.
AWS uses a pay-as-you-go pricing model, Savings Plans, and Reserved Instances for its services.
Azure uses a pay-as-you-go pricing model and Reserved VM Instances for its services.
GCP uses a pay-as-you-go pricing model and Committed Use Discounts (CUDs) for its services.
AWS offers On-Demand Instances, Savings Plans, Reserved Instances, and Spot Instances as pricing models.
Azure offers On-Demand, Reserved Virtual Machine Instances, and Spot Virtual Machines as pricing models.
GCP offers On-Demand, Committed Use Discounts, Sustained Use Discounts, and Preemptible VMs as pricing models.

## Summary
This report compares the major cloud providers (AWS, Azure, GCP) across compute, storage, networking, and pricing models in a structured table.


## Architecture

```mermaid
    N["Networking"] --> N1["AWS: VPC (regional)"]

    P["Pricing"] --> P1["AWS: Savings Plans, Reserved, Spot"]
    P --> P2["Azure: Reserved VM Instances, Spot"]
    P --> P3["GCP: Committed Use Discounts, Preemptible VMs"]
```

## Compute Services
The major cloud providers offer various compute services. AWS offers Elastic Cloud Compute (EC2) [c0], Azure provides Virtual Machines [c1], and GCP offers Compute Engine [c2]. Each service has different instance types, including general purpose, compute optimized, memory optimized, and storage optimized [c3][c4][c5].

## Storage Services
The cloud providers offer object, block, and file storage services. AWS provides S3 (object) [c7], EBS (block) [c10], and EFS/FSx (file) [c13]. Azure offers Blob Storage (object) [c8], Managed Disks (block) [c11], and Azure Files (file) [c14]. GCP provides Cloud Storage (object) [c9], Persistent Disk (block) [c12], and Filestore (file) [c15]. All providers offer storage services with features like versioning and encryption [c16].

## Networking
The providers differ in their virtual network isolation implementations. AWS uses VPCs, Azure uses Virtual Networks, and GCP uses a global VPC model [c18]. GCP's VPC spans across regions, while AWS and Azure have regional VPCs/VNets [c19]. They also differ in their load balancing approaches [c22].

## Pricing Models
The cloud providers use different pricing models. AWS uses pay-as-you-go, Savings Plans, and Reserved Instances [c23]. Azure uses pay-as-you-go and Reserved VM Instances [c24]. GCP uses pay-as-you-go and Committed Use Discounts (CUDs) [c25]. They also offer various pricing options, such as On-Demand, Reserved Instances, and Spot Instances [c26][c27][c28].
